objectives: Interpret the direction and shape of recurrent weights \(W_{ij}\) and input weights \(U_{ij}\), and explain their roles in coupled membrane equations.
Represent a spike train as a sum of Dirac \(\delta\) functions, then use convolution to turn discrete spikes into synaptic input with a time course.
Calculate the mean and variance of the total charge delivered by independent excitatory and inhibitory Poisson inputs within a finite time window.
Compare the large-network scalings \(W\sim 1/N\) and \(W\sim 1/\sqrt N\), explaining why the former suppresses fluctuations and why the latter requires strong E/I cancellation.

Distinguish excitation-dominated, inhibition-dominated, and balanced fluctuation-driven firing from voltage trajectories, and explain why dynamic balance does not mean that the current is exactly zero at every instant.
prerequisiteBridge: A single-neuron equation treats input current \(I(t)\) as a known function. In a network, each neuron's spikes become inputs to other neurons, so their equations are coupled. Adopt the convention that \(W_{ij}\) is the within-network weight from neuron j to neuron i: the first index is the receiver and the second is the sender. For N network neurons, W has shape N×N; M external inputs drive the network through \(U\in \mathbb{R}^{N\times M}\). Writing the index direction first prevents accidental interchange of W and \(W^{\mathrm{T}}\).

The Dirac \(\delta\) is not an ordinary function that takes an infinite numerical value at \(t=0\). It is an idealized event defined by its action under integration: it is zero away from the event, has total area 1, and satisfies \(\int \delta (t-t_{k})g(t)dt=g(t_{k})\). Thus the spike train \(\Delta (t)=\sum _k\delta (t-t_{k})\) has units 1/time. Convolution with a synaptic kernel \(K_{s}\) places a shifted copy of that kernel at every event, producing an ordinary function of time.

Means add for sums of independent random variables, and so do variances. Multiplication by a weight W multiplies the mean by W and the variance by \(W^{2}\). A Poisson count in a short window \(\Delta t\) has both mean and variance \(r\Delta t\). Excitatory weights are positive; inhibition can be represented by a negative weight or by an explicit subtraction from the sum, but one convention must be used consistently throughout a derivation.

Large-N scaling asks how a single connection weight should decrease as N grows so that total input remains meaningful. Its mean depends on N W, whereas its variance depends on \(N W^{2}\). Because these use different powers of W, a population of independent, same-sign inputs cannot keep both quantities finite with one scaling. A balanced network lets large excitatory and inhibitory means cancel while their separately adding variances preserve finite fluctuations.

modules.title: Coupled networks, \(\delta\) spike trains, and synaptic convolution
paragraphs: The network contains N interconnected neurons and M external inputs. \(W_{ij}\) is the recurrent weight \(j\to i\), and \(U_{ij}\) is the weight from external input j→network neuron i. For each i, the membrane equation contains leak, every network sender, and every external sender. Whether diagonal entries of W allow self-connections is a modeling choice. A network is recurrent when W contains feedback paths, not because of where nodes happen to be drawn.

The spike train of neuron j is \(\Delta _{j}(t)=\sum _k\delta (t-t_{k}^{(j)})\). The area of \(\delta\) is 1, so for any smooth g, \(\int \delta (t-t_{k})g(t)dt=g(t_{k})\). Event times \(t_{k}\) are preserved while waveform details are omitted. If time is measured in seconds, \(\Delta\) has units \(s^{-1}\) and cannot be sampled directly as a finite current value.

A synaptic kernel \(K_{s}(t)\) describes how current or conductance changes after one spike. The convolution \((K_{s}*\Delta _{j})(t)=\int K_{s}(t-t')\Delta _{j}(t')dt'\) reduces by the \(\delta\) property to \(\sum _kK_{s}(t-t_{k}^{(j)})\). A causal kernel is zero at negative times, so only past events \(t_{k}\le t\) contribute. Under a linear-synapse approximation, responses to overlapping events add directly.

The coupled equation can be written compactly as C \(dV_{i}/dt=-G_{L}(V_{i}-E_{L})+\sum _jW_{ij}(K_{s}*\Delta _{j})+\sum _jU_{ij}(K_{s}*X_{j})\). Because \(\Delta _{i}\) is itself generated by the threshold–reset dynamics of \(V_{i}\), the system combines continuous voltage states with feedback through discrete events. A network trajectory is fully specified only after initial values, external spike trains, kernels, weights, and event rules are given.

Convolution notation separates “sum over all past spikes” from “the time course after a spike,” so the kernel can be changed without altering network indices. It also exposes the linearity assumption. If synapses saturate, facilitate over the short term, or have inhibitory conductance that depends on V, a single fixed kernel and simple superposition may fail; additional synaptic state variables or conductance-based currents are then needed.
keyPoints: The first index of \(W_{ij}\) is receiver i; the second is sender j.
A \(\delta\) spike train is an event distribution that becomes an ordinary time process after convolution with a kernel.
Network equations combine continuous membrane states with discrete feedback events generated by thresholds.

derivation.title: Using the sifting property of \(\delta\) to reduce a convolution to a sum of kernels
derivation.setup: Sender j spikes at times \(t_{k}^{(j)}\), with \(\Delta _{j}(t)=\sum _k\delta (t-t_{k}^{(j)})\); define its synaptic response as \(I_{j}=K_{s}*\Delta _{j}\).

steps.title: Write the convolution definition
steps.explanation: Integrate the product of the kernel and spike train over every possible event time t'.

steps.title: Substitute the event sum
steps.explanation: Substitute \(\Delta _{j}(t')=\sum _k\delta (t'-t_{k}^{(j)})\) and interchange integration with the finite or convergent sum.

steps.title: Apply the sifting property
steps.explanation: \(\delta\) fixes t' at \(t_{k}^{(j)}\), turning each term into \(K_{s}(t-t_{k}^{(j)})\).

steps.title: Obtain the event representation
steps.explanation: The full synaptic trajectory is the linear superposition of kernels triggered by all events.

steps.title: Impose causality
steps.explanation: If \(K_{s}(u)=0\) for \(u<0\), terms from future events \(t_{k}>t\) vanish automatically.

symbolNotes: t is the present observation time, t' is a dummy integration variable, and \(t_{k}^{(j)}\) is the time of sender j's kth spike.

The kernel and weight must be defined together. If \(K_{s}\) is dimensionless and peak-normalized, W is a current amplitude. If \(K_{s}\) is area-normalized with units 1/time, W is an impulse area or charge, and W \(K_{s}\) has units of current.
derivation.unitsCheck: \(\Delta\) has units 1/s, while the convolution integral contributes dt' with units s, so \(K_{s}*\Delta\) has the same units as \(K_{s}\). Multiplication by W must then produce the current units required by the membrane equation.
derivation.limitCheck: With no spikes, the sum is empty and the response is zero. As the kernel approaches \(\delta\), the convolution approaches the unsmoothed spike train. Responses add in amplitude when identical spikes coincide.

workedExample.title: Superposition of exponential kernels from two spikes
workedExample.problem: Spikes occur at 1 ms and 3 ms. This example calculates only the kernel shape, using the dimensionless, peak-normalized causal kernel \(K(u)=e^{-u/2 ms}H(u)\); an external weight supplies the physical current amplitude. Find the dimensionless total kernel response at \(t=2 \mathrm{ms}\) and 4 ms.
steps: At \(t=2 \mathrm{ms}\), the delay from the 1 ms spike is 1 ms, contributing \(e^{-1/2}\approx 0.6065\). The 3 ms spike has not yet occurred and contributes 0.
Thus the total response at \(t=2 \mathrm{ms}\) is approximately 0.6065.
At \(t=4 \mathrm{ms}\), the two delays are 3 ms and 1 ms, contributing \(e^{-3/2}\approx 0.2231\) and \(e^{-1/2}\approx 0.6065\).
workedExample.result: The response is approximately 0.6065 at 2 ms and 0.8296 at 4 ms.
workedExample.sanityCheck: After the second spike, the total response can rise; each individual exponential contribution is at most 1, its value at the event.

pitfalls: Reading \(W_{ij}\) as \(i\to j\) and thereby transposing the direction of network connections.
Allowing future spikes to affect the present state by using a noncausal kernel.
Treating the height of \(\delta\) as a physical current amplitude and ignoring conventions for area and weight units.

modules.title: Mean, variance, and the failure of 1/N scaling for stochastic E/I input
paragraphs: Consider \(N_{E}\) excitatory inputs, each with rate \(r_{E}\) and weight \(W_{E}>0\), and \(N_{I}\) inhibitory inputs, each with rate \(r_{I}\) and magnitude \(W_{I}>0\) that is subtracted from total charge. Temporarily ignore kernel shape and let the count of each input during \(\Delta t\) be Poisson. Total charge is \(Q=\sum _E W_{E} K_{j}-\sum _I W_{I} K_{j}\). The sign affects the mean, but squared weights make excitatory and inhibitory fluctuations both contribute positively to variance.

Using \(E[K]=\operatorname{Var}(K)=r\Delta t\) gives \(E[Q]=(N_{\mathrm{EW},Er,E}-N_{\mathrm{IW},Ir,I})\Delta t\). Independence gives \(\operatorname{Var}(Q)=(N_{\mathrm{EW},E}^{2}r_{E}+N_{\mathrm{IW},I}^{2}r_{I})\Delta t\). E/I contributions can cancel in the mean, but their variances cannot cancel merely because their signs differ. If inputs are correlated, pairwise covariance terms must be added and the independent formula may underestimate or otherwise alter the fluctuations.

First try \(W_{E}\),\(W_{I}\sim 1/N\). Each population \(\operatorname{mean} N W\) remains \(O(1)\), so it does not diverge even without precise cancellation. But variance \(N W^{2}\sim 1/N\to 0\) and standard deviation∼\(1/\sqrt N\to 0\). Input to a large network becomes almost a deterministic mean current. A deterministic downstream LIF neuron then fires regularly if the mean is above threshold and remains silent if it is below, rather than preserving Poisson-like trial variability.

This does not mean fluctuations are exactly zero at finite N; it means that they systematically shrink as connectivity grows. Kernel smoothing further averages rapid fluctuations in time without changing the essential appearance of squared weights in the variance. To identify the simulated limit, measure means and variances across several N values instead of inspecting a voltage trace at one network size.

Same-sign independent input alone cannot keep both mean and fluctuations finite. \(W\sim 1/N\) preserves the mean but loses the variance, whereas \(W\sim 1/\sqrt N\) preserves the variance but makes each population mean grow as \(\sqrt N\). The solution is cancellation between the large excitatory and inhibitory means, which leads to the balanced state on the next step. This cancellation affects the signed first moment, not the variance created by independent events. Precisely because means and variances obey different addition rules, balance can prevent divergence while retaining fluctuations.
keyPoints: The E/I mean is a signed difference, whereas independent variances add through squared weights.
With \(W\sim 1/N\), the mean is \(O(1)\) and the variance is \(O(1/N)\), so stochastic fluctuations vanish at large N.
Finite fluctuations require stronger \(1/\sqrt N\) weights and cancellation between E/I means.

derivation.title: Mean and variance of convergent Poisson input
derivation.setup: Within \(\Delta t\), excitatory counts \(K_{j}^E\sim \operatorname{Poisson}(r_{E}\Delta t)\) and inhibitory counts \(K_{j}^I\sim \operatorname{Poisson}(r_{I}\Delta t)\), with all inputs independent.

steps.title: Write the total charge
steps.explanation: Excitatory events add with \(+W_{E}\); inhibitory events add with \(-W_{I}\).

steps.title: Calculate the mean
steps.explanation: Expectation is linear, and each Poisson mean is \(r\Delta t\).

steps.title: Calculate the variance
steps.explanation: Variances of independent terms add. Squaring the negative sign makes its contribution positive, and Poisson variance equals its mean.

steps.title: Insert the 1/N scaling
steps.explanation: If \(N_{E}\) and \(N_{I}\) are both of order N and \(W\sim N^{-1}\), each mean is \(O(1)\) and the variance is \(O(N^{-1})\).

steps.title: Interpret the voltage consequence
steps.explanation: Input standard deviation is \(O(N^{-1}/^{2})\). At large N, voltage responds mainly to the deterministic mean and random threshold crossings disappear.

symbolNotes: \(W_{I}\) is defined as a positive magnitude and explicitly carries a minus sign in Q. Negative weights are an equivalent convention, but the minus sign must not be applied twice.
\(\Delta t\) must be short enough that the rate is approximately constant; K is the event count in that window.
derivation.unitsCheck: If W is charge per spike, Q is charge. Because \(r\Delta t\) is dimensionless, the mean has units of charge and the variance has units of charge squared.
derivation.limitCheck: When \(N_{E}=N_{I}\), \(W_{E}=W_{I}\), and \(r_{E}=r_{I}\), the mean is zero but the variance is the sum of two positive population contributions. As \(N\to \infty\) with \(W\sim 1/N\), this variance approaches zero.

workedExample.title: Fluctuations under 1/N scaling with ten thousand inputs
workedExample.problem: Let \(N_{E}=N_{I}=10000\), \(r_{E}=r_{I}=10 \mathrm{Hz}\), \(\Delta t=1 \mathrm{ms}\), and \(W_{E}=W_{I}=1/N\) in arbitrary units. Calculate each population's mean magnitude, the net mean, total variance, and standard deviation.
steps: \(W=1/10000=10^{-4}\). The mean of either population is NWr\(\Delta t=10000\cdot 10^{-4}\cdot 10\cdot 0.001=0.01\).
The variance of either population is \(N W^{2}\) \(r\Delta t=10000\cdot 10^{-8}\cdot 10\cdot 0.001=10^{-6}\).
Total variance is \(2\times 10^{-6}\), and standard deviation is \(\operatorname{sqrt}(2\times 10^{-6})\approx 0.001414\).
workedExample.result: The two population means are each 0.01 and cancel. Total standard deviation is only about 0.00141 and continues to decrease as N grows.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Variance must remain positive even when E/I means cancel exactly. The standard deviation is about 14% of the single-population \(\operatorname{mean} 0.01\).

pitfalls: Keeping the inhibitory minus sign in the variance formula and obtaining a potentially negative variance.
Applying weight scaling only to the mean and failing to use \(W^{2}\) in the variance.
Inferring from one irregular trajectory in a finite network that the large-N limit must also remain irregular.

modules.title: Strong \(1/\sqrt N\) coupling, E/I balance, and irregular spiking
paragraphs: If weights scale as \(W\sim 1/\sqrt N\), variance \(N W^{2}\sim O(1)\), so total-input standard deviation remains finite as N grows. The cost is that each population \(\operatorname{mean} N W\sim \sqrt N\) becomes large. For the net mean to stay \(O(1)\), leading-order balance \(N_{\mathrm{EW},Er,E}\approx N_{\mathrm{IW},Ir,I}\) is required: two \(O(\sqrt N)\) terms cancel and leave only a finite residual.

Balance does not require excitatory and inhibitory currents to be exactly equal in every millisecond. It constrains conditional means or leading terms at a large scale; instantaneous differences between independent spikes retain \(O(1)\) fluctuations. Those differences make LIF voltage wander irregularly and occasionally cross threshold. With excitation dominance, the mean slope remains upward and firing is more regular. With inhibition dominance, voltage stays below threshold. In the balanced state, fluctuations drive threshold crossings at irregular intervals.

The balance condition is sensitive to relative mismatch. Each canceled term is \(O(\sqrt N)\), so if their relative mismatch remains constant, the net input also grows as \(\sqrt N\). Through \(E\to I\), \(I\to E\), recurrent connections, and external drive, network dynamics must adjust firing rates so that mean inhibition tracks mean excitation. Dynamic balance is a network-generated state, not merely a manual choice of equal external rates.

The dynamic-balance framework cited in the source lecture shows that recurrent E/I networks can maintain this cancellation spontaneously and produce nearly Poisson variability. “Nearly” should be tested using ISIs, Fano factors, correlations, and state dependence. Irregular firing can also arise from external noise or slow modulation, so a balanced network is a candidate mechanism, not something uniquely identified by one jagged voltage trace.

Scaling analysis gives testable simulation predictions. Change K or N while scaling weights as \(1/\sqrt K\), and record the mean absolute E and I magnitudes, net mean, variance, and firing CV. In the correct balanced limit, E and I means grow as \(\sqrt K\) and cancel, while net mean and variance remain \(O(1)\). Plotting only net current hides the large underlying cancellation.
keyPoints: \(W\sim 1/\sqrt N\) keeps variance \(O(1)\) but makes the separate E and I means \(O(\sqrt N)\).
Balance cancels the leading-order mean while retaining instantaneous fluctuations; it is not zero current at every moment.
Recurrent feedback can dynamically adjust E/I rates and place a strongly coupled network in an irregular balanced state.

derivation.title: Finite variance and the balance condition under \(1/\sqrt N\) scaling
derivation.setup: Let \(N_{E}=a_{\mathrm{EN}}\), \(N_{I}=a_{\mathrm{IN}}\), \(W_{E}=w_{E}/\sqrt N\), and \(W_{I}=w_{I}/\sqrt N\), while rates and \(\Delta t\) remain independent of N.

steps.title: Substitute into the mean
steps.explanation: The E-population mean is \(a_{E}\sqrt N\) \(w_{Er,E}\Delta t\), with an analogous I-population term. The leading net mean is \(\sqrt N\) times their difference.

steps.title: Impose leading-order balance
steps.explanation: To prevent divergence of the net mean, require \(a_{Ew,Er,E}-a_{Iw,Ir,I}=O(N^{-1/2})\); the leading terms are equal in the limit.

steps.title: Interpret the remaining fluctuations
steps.explanation: Cancellation of leading mean terms does not change the positive sum of independent variances, so standard deviation remains \(O(1)\).

steps.title: Connect to irregular threshold crossings
steps.explanation: A finite net mean combined with finite fluctuations lets voltage cross threshold at irregular times, instead of being completely deterministic or completely silent.

symbolNotes: \(a_{E}\) and \(a_{I}\) are the fractions of the N inputs belonging to each class; \(w_{E}\) and \(w_{I}\) are the scaled strengths that do not change with N.
“≈” denotes leading-order balance at large N. A finite network can retain an \(O(1)\) net residual.
derivation.unitsCheck: a and N are dimensionless; \(w/\sqrt N\) inherits the units of a single-synapse weight. Mean and variance units are as in the preceding module.
derivation.limitCheck: If the balance difference is a fixed nonzero constant, the net mean diverges as \(\sqrt N\). If the weights are changed to 1/N, the variance again approaches zero.

workedExample.title: Balancing the same ten thousand inputs under \(1/\sqrt N\) scaling
workedExample.problem: Continue with \(N_{E}=N_{I}=10000\), \(r=10 \mathrm{Hz}\), and \(\Delta t=1 \mathrm{ms}\), but set \(W=1/\sqrt N=0.01\). The E/I means are exactly equal. Calculate each population mean, net mean, total variance, and standard deviation.
steps: The mean of either population is \(10000\cdot 0.01\cdot 10\cdot 0.001=1\).
By symmetry the net mean is \(1-1=0\), but each term is 100 times larger than its value 0.01 under 1/N scaling.
The variance of either population is \(10000\cdot 0.01^{2}\cdot 10\cdot 0.001=0.01\).
Total variance is 0.02, and standard deviation is \(\operatorname{sqrt}(0.02)\approx 0.1414\), remaining finite to leading order as N changes.
workedExample.result: The strong E/I means are each 1 and cancel, leaving net \(\operatorname{mean} 0\). Total standard deviation is about 0.141, preserving fluctuations that can drive voltage.
workedExample.sanityCheck: Changing from 1/N to \(1/\sqrt N\) makes a single weight 100 times larger and variance 10000 times larger, from \(2\times 10^{-6}\) to 0.02.

pitfalls: Interpreting balance as exact equality of E and I current at every instant and therefore predicting zero fluctuations.
Plotting only the net E+I curve without separately verifying the two large components and their N scaling.
Treating a balanced network as the unique cause of irregular firing without comparing external noise and nonstationary drive.
